elements.text: Synthesis of Poly(ester amide)s by the Melt Polycondensation of Semiaromatic Polyesters with Ethanolamine and Their Characterization
HATSUHIKO HARASHINA,<sup>1,2</sup> TOSHIO NAKANE,<sup>2</sup> TAKAHITO ITOH<sup>1</sup>
<sup>1</sup>Division of Chemistry for Materials, Graduate School of Engineering, Mie University, 1577 Kurima Machiya-Cho, Tsu-Shi, Mie 514-8507, Japan
<sup>2</sup>Polyplastics Co., Ltd., 973 Miyajima, Fuji-Shi, Shizuoka 416-8533, Japan
Received 29 September 2006; accepted 4 January 2007
Published online in Wiley InterScience (www.interscience.wiley.com).

ABSTRACT: Semiaromatic poly(ester amide)s (PEAs) were synthesized by the melt polycondensation of ethanolamine (EA) derivatives with dimethyl terephthalate and ethylene glycol in the presence of tetrabutyl titanate as a catalyst, and their crystallization and thermal properties were investigated. The introduction of an amide group into a semiaromatic polyester such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) produced PEAs (EA-modified PET polymers) with an increase in the melting point. However, these PEAs were found to decompose at a lower temperature than PET on the basis of TGA. Moreover, direct pyrolysis/mass spectrometry measurements suggested that an initial step of the thermal decomposition was a b-CH hydrogen-transfer reaction via a six-member ring transition state at the ester–ethylene–amide unit, at which carbon– oxygen bond scission took place to yield carboxyl and N-vinylamide end groups. Furthermore, molecular orbital calculations using trimer models bis[2-[[4-(methoxycarbonyl)benzoyl]oxy]ethyl]terephthalate, N-[2-[[4-(methoxycarbonyl)benzoyl]oxy]ethyl]-4- [2-[[4-(methoxycarbonyl)benzoyl]oxy]ethyloxycarbonyl]benzamide, and N,N0-bis[2-[[4- (methoxycarbonyl)benzoyl]oxy]ethyl]terephthalamide strongly supported the idea that the b-CH hydrogen-transfer reaction in the thermal decomposition of PEAs might occur more easily at the methylene group next to the amide group in an ester–ethylene–amide unit rather than at the methylene group next to the ester group in an ester–ethylene–ester unit. Keywords: crystallization; ethanolamine; melt polycondensation; modification; molecular orbital calculation; polyamides; polyaromatics; poly(ester amide); polyesters; pyrolysis/mass spectrometry; synthesis; thermal analysis; thermal decomposition; thermal properties
INTRODUCTION

Semiaromatic polyesters such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) and poly(butylene terephthalate) have superior mechanical, thermal, and chemical properties, and they have been used in many industrial fields as engineering plastics. On the other hand, polyamides, typically represented by nylon-6 and nylon-6,6, also possess good mechanical and physical properties. In particular, semiaromatic polyamides such as poly(hexamethylene terephthalamide) and poly(nonamethylene terephthalamide) have better thermal properties than the corresponding semiaromatic polyesters. One of the methods of improving the thermal properties of polyesters, including aliphatic, aliphatic–aromatic, and aromatic polyesters, is to introduce some thermally stable groups, such as amide groups, into the main chains of the polyesters. Improvements of the mechanical and thermal properties and crystallinity of polymers by the incorporation of a certain amount of amide groups into the main chains of polyesters have been reported.<sup>1–19</sup> Ethanolamine (EA) has been used as an amide group source in such improvements in industry, and several synthesis methods for EA-based semiaromatic poly(ester amide)s (PEAs) have been proposed.<sup>20–23</sup> However, most works reported previously were related to synthesis methods for EA-modified PET polymers using activated aromatic dicarboxylic acids, but their thermal properties were not studied in detail. In this work, we describe the synthesis of semiaromatic PEAs by melt polycondensation, using EA as a monomer or comonomer instead of an ethylene glycol (EG) component in PET, and their crystallization and thermal properties. Furthermore, the thermal decomposition behavior of the PEAs is discussed on the basis of the application of molecular orbital (MO) calculations to trimer models for the PET and PEAs.

elements.text: EXPERIMENTAL
Materials
Commercial EA, EG, dimethyl terephthalate (DMT), dimethyl isophthalate (DMI), and tetrabutyl titanate (all products from Tokyo Kasei Kogyo Co., Ltd.) were used without further purification.
Synthesis of Amide Intermediates

N,N0-Bis(2-hydroxyethyl)terephthalamide (BHTA; mp 226–228 8C, lit.<sup>23</sup> 225–227 8C), used with method A in Scheme 1, was prepared by the aminolysis reaction (i.e., amidation) of EA with DMT at 80 8C for 8 h and obtained as colorless crystals by recrystallization from methanol. Other diamide intermediates (BHTA and N,N0-bis(2- hydroxyethyl)isophthalamide; BHIA, used with method B, were synthesized by the aminolysis reaction of DMT or DMI with EA; 0.03 mol of DMT or DMI and 0.06 mol of EA were heated in 20 mL of EG at 100 8C for 1 h without a catalyst. Also, the monoamide intermediates methyl 4-[[(2- hydroxyethyl)amino]carbony]benzoate (M4HB) and methyl 3-[[(2-hydroxyethyl)amino]carbony]- benzoate (M3HB), used with method B, were prepared by the dropwise addition of 0.06 mol of EA into 0.06 mol of DMT or DMI in 40 mL of EG with stirring to suppress the formation of BHTA or BHIA, followed by heating at ${ 1 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$for 1 h. Each EG solution, containing various amide intermediates, was added to the ester-exchange reaction mixture of DMT and EG without further isolation and purification, as shown Scheme 1.

elements.text: Synthesis of PEAs

PEAs were prepared by conventional melt polycondensation via two methods (methods A and B), as shown in Scheme 1; each EG solution, containing amide intermediates, without further purification or isolation was added to the preproduct of PET, which was derived from the ester-exchange reaction of DMT with EG in the presence of tetrabutyl titanate.

Method A was used for the synthesis of PEAs with amide contents of 3, 10, 20, 40, and 50 mol %, as listed in Tables 1 and 2. DMT (1.0 mol), EG (1.5 mol), and tetrabutyl titanate (0.41 mmol) as a catalyst were mixed in an autoclave equipped with a mechanical stirrer, condenser, and nitrogen inlet, and the mixture was reacted at 120 8C for 2 h. Then, 0.03, 0.11, 0.25, 0.67, or 1.0 mol of BHTA crystals as an diamide intermediate was added to the ester-exchange reaction mixture (preproduct of PET), and the mixture was gradually heated to 250 8C with stirring for 2 h. On the other hand, in method B, an EG solution containing diamide and monoamide intermediates (0.03 mol of BHTA or BHIA and 0.06 mol of M4HB or M3HB) was added to the preproduct of PET, and the resulting mixture was polymerized with the same procedure of method A to obtain PEAs with an amide content of 3 mol % (PEAs IV, V, VI, and VII), as listed in Table 2. Also, PET (I) was prepared by the ester-exchange reaction and melt polycondensation of EG with DMT in the presence of tetrabutyl titanate without any amide intermediate.
Measurements

The number-average $( M _ { \mathrm { n } } )$and weight-average $( M _ { \mathrm { w } } )$molecular weights and molecular weight distributions $( M _ { \mathrm { w } } / M _ { \mathrm { n } } )$of the polymers were determined by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) on a Tosoh HPLC-8020 equipped with a Tosoh ultraviolet (254-nm) detector, a refractive-index detector, and a gel column combination (Shodex AD polystyrene 800p, 803s, 805/s, and 807/s) with 1,1,1,3,3,3-hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) as an eluent at a flow rate of 0.85 mL/min and with polystyrene standards for calibration at $4 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$. The melting temperature $( T _ { \mathbf { m } } )$cold crystallization temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { { c } } } )$recrystallization temperature $( T _ { \mathbf { r } } )$, heat of crystallization $( \Delta H _ { \mathrm { m } } )$, and glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$of the polymers were measured with a PerkinElmer DSC 7 analyzer at heating/cooling rates of 10 8C/min with a holding time of 3 min at $3 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$under a nitrogen atmosphere. The DSC samples of PEAs were heated quickly to $3 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and held for 3 min. Then, they were cooled quickly $( > 5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { \textdegree C / m i n } )$to room temperature to obtain quenched amorphous PEA samples. The DSC scans of the first heating–cooling cycle of these PEAs were recorded. The initial decomposition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { i } } )$and onset of decomposition curves were determined with a PerkinElmer TGA 7 analyzer at a heating rate of 10 8C/min under a nitrogen atmosphere.
Thermal Decomposition Analysis

The thermal decomposition products of the polymers were determined by direct pyrolysis/mass spectrometry (DPMS) measurements with a Hitachi model M-2000 mass spectrometer with scanning in the region of m/z 60–460 or m/z 60–660. Perfluorokerosene was used for computer calibration. The polymer sample was introduced into a chamber with a direct insertion probe, and the chamber was heated from 30 to $4 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$at a heating rate of 10 8C/min. The volatile pyrolysis products were ionized by positive chemical ionization (CI) with an isobutene.
Computational Methods

MO calculations were carried out with a semiempirical MO package program (MOPAC 2000).<sup>24</sup> All molecular structures of the model molecules used in this work were optimized with the AM1 Hamiltonian, and their frontier electron distributions and densities were calculated for the evaluation of the thermal degradability of PEAs.<sup>25</sup>
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Melt Polycondensation

PEAs with different amounts of amide groups (PEAs IIa–IId) were prepared by method A, and their thermal properties are summarized in Table 1, together with the corresponding ones of PET. PEAs with an amide content of 3 mol % (PEAs IIIa–IIc and IV–VII) were prepared by methods A and B, and their thermal properties, molecular weights, and molecular weight distributions were summarized in Table 2, together with the corresponding ones of PET.

PEAs IIa–IIc were crystalline polymers, whereas PEA IId with an amide content of50 mol % was amorphous and also partially insoluble in HFIP. The PEAs with an amide content of 3 mol % had $M _ { \mathrm { n } }$values in the range of $1 5 , 8 0 0 { - } 2 7 , 0 0 0 , M _ { \mathrm { w } }$values in the range of $5 6 , 0 0 0 { - } 9 6 , 0 0 0 ,$, and molecular weight distributions $( M _ { \mathrm { w } } / M _ { \mathrm { n } } )$of3.3–3.6 for method A and of 2.9–3.2 for method B, which were broader than that $( M _ { \mathrm { w } } / M _ { \mathrm { n } } = 2 . 4 )$ofPET.
Thermal Behavior

$T _ { \mathrm { m } } , T _ { \mathrm { g } } , T _ { \mathrm { c } } , T _ { \mathrm { r } } ,$and $\Delta H _ { \mathbf { m } }$of the PEAs with amide contents as high as 10, 20, 40, and 50 mol % and of those with amide contents as low as 3 mol % were determined by DSC measurements and are summarized in Tables 1 and 2, respectively. $T _ { \mathbf { m } }$of the PEAs increased with increasing amide content in the polymers (Table 1). However, $T _ { \mathbf { m } }$of PEA IId was not clearly observed, although $T _ { \mathbf { m } }$of the PEA prepared by solution polycondensation at a temperature as low as 30 8C was reported to be 332 8C.<sup>23</sup> DSC curves for PEAs IIIa–IIIc and

All PEAs showed almost the same $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$value of $8 0 \ \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$although they had significantly different values of $T _ { \mathrm { m } } , T _ { \mathrm { c } }$and $T _ { \mathbf { r } } ,$depending on the preparation method and the chemical structure. A series of PEAs with 3 mol % amide had poly(oxyethyleneoxyterephthaloyl) segments as the main components. The influence of such segments is reflected by $T _ { \mathbf { m } }$and $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$of those PEAs, which showed values almost equivalent to those of PET. On the other hand, it is thought that 3 mol % amide could significantly influence the crystallization behavior, including $T _ { \mathbf { r } }$and $T _ { \mathrm { c } } ,$and the mobility of the poly(oxyethyleneoxyterephthaloyl) segments to give PEAs having the crystallization rate and the degree of crystallinity.

From the data of $T _ { \mathbf { r } }$and the degree of supercooling $( \Delta T = T _ { \mathrm { m } } - T _ { \mathrm { r } } )$in Figure 1 and Table 2, the crystallization rates of PEAs IIIa–IIIc derived from BHTA were found to be faster than that of PET. On the other hand, Figure 2 shows that the crystallization behavior of various PEAs was strongly dependent on their polymer structures as well as the polymerization methods. It was reported that in the melt blending of PET and nylon-6,6 in the presence ofp-toluenesulfonic acid as an acidic catalyst, an ester–amide interchange reaction took place to afford polyester– polyamide copolymers with higher crystallinity.<sup>26</sup> It is considered, therefore, that the different crystallization behaviors and the broadening of the molecular weight distribution of GPC for PEAs may come from the somewhat disordered sequences, which take place during the ester–amide interchange reaction in melt polycondensation in the presence of tetrabutyl titanate as a catalyst.
Thermal Stability of PEAs

The thermogravimetric curves of PET and PEAs IIa–IId are shown in Figure $^ { 3 , }$and their $T _ { \mathrm { i } }$and decomposition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { d } } )$values are summarized in Table 1.

$T _ { \mathrm { i } }$and $T _ { \mathrm { d } }$of PEAs IIa–IId decreased significantly with increasing amide content in the polymers, and PEA IId with an amide content of 50 mol % showed a $T _ { \mathrm { i } }$value of 280 8C and a $T _ { \mathrm { d } }$value of $3 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$. On the other hand, PET had the corresponding temperatures of 366 and 409 ${ } ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } .$respectively. The PEAs with amide contents higher than 10 mol % had poor thermal stability in comparison with PET.

elements.text: Mechanism of the Thermal Decomposition of PEAs

To clarify the poor thermal stability of PEAs derived from EA, their thermal decomposition products were analyzed by DPMS. This DPMS technique has the important advantage of involving a pyrolysis reaction under a high vacuum. Therefore, the pyrolysis products are volatized rapidly and removed immediately from the hot area to be mildly ionized and detected. In such an ideal state, molecular collisions might be suppressed to a low probability, and side reactions could also be significantly inhibited, so primary fragments could be detected almost exclusively. The mass spectrum obtained by this method is therefore attributable to many components of primary volatile pyrolysis products. Figure 4 shows the DPMS spectra of decomposition products of PEA IId obtained at three different temperatures: 180, 200, and 230 8C.

The DPMS spectra of PEA IId exhibited two main peaks at m/z 217 (AHþ) and $m / z = 1 4 8$(BHþ) assignable to N,N0-divinyl terephthalamide and N-vinyl benzamide, respectively, and also a peak at $m / z = 1 9 2 ~ \mathrm { ( C H ^ { + } ) }$assignable to PEA, indicating the formation of a vinylamide compound with a cyclic monomeric structure. The DPMS spectra of the decomposition products for PEA IIIb with an amide content of 3 mol % in the different temperature ranges of 310–340, 340– 360, and $3 6 0 { - } 3 8 0 \ { \textdegree } \mathbf { C }$are shown in Figure 5.

In the temperature region of $3 1 0 \mathrm { - } 3 4 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$, the peaks observed at m/z 148 (BHþ), m/z 192 $( \mathrm { C H ^ { + } } ) ,$and $m / z = 5 7 7$were assigned to N-vinyl benzamide, a cyclic monomeric compound of PEA,

In a higher temperature range of $3 6 0 \mathrm { - } 3 8 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$, peaks at $m / z = 1 4 9 ~ ( \mathrm { D H ^ { + } } )$and $m / z = 2 1 9 ~ ( \mathrm { E H ^ { + } } )$were observed, and they could be assigned to vinyl benzoate and divinyl terephthalate formed from the PET sequence. It has been reported that the thermal decomposition mechanism of aliphatic–aromatic polyesters such as PET and poly(butylene terephthalate) is a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process via a six-membered ring transition state in the ethylene–ester unit, at which carbon–oxygen bond scission takes place to yield carboxyl and vinyl ester end groups<sup>27–30</sup> [Scheme 2(a)]. Montaudo et al.<sup>31</sup> concluded that the primary thermal decomposition process of some aliphatic–aromatic polyamides including poly(ethylene terephthalamide) proceeds via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process accompanying carbon–nitrogen bond scission in the ethylene–amide unit with the formation of thermal decomposition products having amide and N-vinylamide end groups [Scheme 2(b)]. For PEA IId with an amide content of 50 mol %, two thermal decomposition pathways via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process are possible in the ester– ethylene–amide unit [Scheme 2(c)].

The DPMS analysis of PEA suggests strongly that its primary thermal decomposition proceeds via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer reaction accompanying carbon–oxygen bond scission in the ester– ethylene–amide unit via a six-membered ring transition state to form carboxyl and N-vinylamide end groups. On the other hand, for the PEAs (EA-modified PETs) containing lower amide contents, at a lower temperature, the ester–ethylene–amide unit in the polymer decomposes exclusively via a hydrogen-transfer process from the carbon next to the amide group. Then, at a higher temperature, the following thermal decomposition in the ester–ethylene–ester unit took place via a b-CH hydrogen-transfer process to give the thermally decomposed products with carboxyl and vinyl ester end groups.

elements.text: MO Calculations

PEAs prepared in this work were found to decompose at lower temperatures than PET. For example, PEA IId decomposed at 350 8C, whereas PET did at 409 8C (Table 1). Moreover, in the DPMS analysis, PEAs decomposed via a b-CH hydrogentransfer process to give exclusively decomposition products with an N-vinylamide end group. MO calculation is a powerful tool for the theoretical prediction of chemical reactivities. Therefore, we applied this MO calculation method to the prediction of the specific decomposition behavior of PEAs. Previously, the thermal decomposition process for PET and poly(butylene terephthalate) with model compounds such as ethylene dibenzoate and 1,4-butylene dibenzoate was reported.<sup>32–34</sup> As the appropriate model compounds for the PEAs and PET, we selected the following three trimer models: bis[2-[[4-(methoxycarbonyl)- benzoyl]oxy]ethyl] terephthalate (I), N-[2-[[4- (methoxycarbonyl)benzoyl]oxy]ethyl]-4-[2-[[4-(methoxycarbonyl)benzoyl]oxy]ethyloxycarbonyl]benzamide (II) and N,N0-bis[2-[[4-(methoxycarbonyl)- benzoyl]oxy]ethyl]terephthalamide (III). The most stable structures of each trimer model were determined by optimization using the AM1 Hamiltonian. Figure 6 shows the geometrically stable Corey–Pauling–Koltun (CPK) structures of the trimer models. The trimer model (I) for PET has a considerable extended structure with a coplanarity of the benzene ring. The other two trimer models (II and III) for the PEAs have a remarkably bent and twisted conformation at the amide group because of its partial double-bond character. The existence of such a disordered unit or sequence should determine the final structure in the main chain of PEAs. It is, therefore, thought that despite a strong intermolecular interaction due to the hydrogen bond between the amide groups, an unexpected behavior for the crystallization was observed.

On the basis of the optimized structures of the trimer models, frontier orbitals of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) ofthe trimer models were calculated and are depicted in Figure 7.

elements.text: In the trimer model (I) for PET, all the HOMO electrons were localized on the benzene ring. On the other hand, in the trimer model (II) for PEA IId, a considerable number of HOMO electrons were distributed on the ester–ethylene–amide unit of the reaction center. In the trimer model (III) having both ester–ethylene–amide and ester– ethylene–ester units in the molecule, HOMO electrons were distributed on the ester–ethylene–amide unit rather than on the ester–ethylene–ester unit. Figure 8 shows the HOMO electron densities of four protons in the ethylene unit for the three trimer models.

It was found that the electron density (0.034 for trimer model II and 0.012 and 0.013 for trimer model III) of a proton in the methylene group next to the amide group was higher than those of the other three protons. Such a proton exhibited the highest reactivity among the four protons in the ethylene unit. Therefore, it was expected that in the thermal degradation reaction via a sixmembered cyclic transition state (a concerted reaction), a hydride-transfer reaction might take place easily to yield products with both carboxyl and vinyl amide end groups. The MO calculation results obtained on the basis of the frontier electron densities for the trimer models could explain well the specific thermal degradation behavior of the PEAs prepared in this work.
CONCLUSIONS
Various semiaromatic PEAs were synthesized by the melt polycondensation of EA derivatives with

DMT and EG in the presence of tetrabutyl titanate. The introduction of an amide group with EA into a semiaromatic polyester was effective in increasing $T _ { \mathbf { m } } .$. However, PEAs with amide contents higher than 10 mol % decomposed at significantly lower temperatures than PET. The initial primary step in the thermal decomposition of PEAs was confirmed to be a b-CH hydrogen transfer reaction accompanying carbon–oxygen bond scission in the ester–ethylene–amide unit via a six-membered ring transition state that yielded carboxyl and N-vinylamide end groups. Furthermore, the specific thermal decomposition behavior of PEAs was explained well by both the HOMO electron distributions and the frontier electron densities for the trimer models.
